choice: The verdict names the model to use on these series and how sure that is. p_best is the share of resamples of the series in which the model is the best one: 0.9 means it wins 9 times out of 10 when the set of series is redrawn. expected_loss_rel is how much worse than the best it is on average, counting the cases where another model wins: 0.01 means 1% worse.

claim.verified is true only when the winner's lead over the runner-up survives a test whose false-alarm rate was checked on this very data. winners_curse is the score of the chosen model on windows or series it was not chosen on: the honest number to expect next time.
ladder: Every number is skill in nats over repeating the last value: log(MSE of repeating the last value / MSE). Higher is better, 0 means no better than repeating the last value, negative means worse. x nats means a squared error lower by 1 - e^-x (column *_pct) or e^x times smaller: 0.1 nats is about 10% lower, 0.7 about 50% lower (2 times smaller), 2.3 about 90% lower (10 times smaller), 4.6 about 99% lower (100 times smaller).

The gains add up: total = F + L + beyond_linear. F is what the best simple rule gets (drift, seasonal naive, the mean, ... chosen per series on the history). L is what a linear model fitted on the history adds on top of that rule. beyond_linear is what the model adds on top of the linear model. F and L describe the data, not any model; beyond_linear and total belong to the model.

group is the forecast step: 1 is one step ahead, 2-4 and 5+ further ahead. The row 'all' pools squared errors over every step, so it is dominated by the far steps, where errors are largest; it is not the average of the other rows.

*_se is the standard error over series: a value within about two standard errors of 0 is not distinguishable from 0. saturated says whether giving the linear model more memory had stopped helping it on the history; if not, L is a lower bound.

verdict, per group: 'beyond linear' (the model beats the linear model by more than twice the standard error and more than the offset a fitted linear model leaves, with a saturated reference), 'no better than linear' (it does not beat it at all), 'not shown' (ahead, but not by enough), 'reference not saturated'. credited is the overall answer: 'beyond linear' only if every group says so.

caveats.message: synthetic:lorenz: mean passes the beyond-linear test only at steps 5+; the paper's rule counts it only when it holds in every horizon group, because a run reads many cells and one passing alone can be chance

synthetic:rossler: the linear reference is not saturated at steps 1, 2-4, 5+ (more memory still helped it by 0.82 nats on the history): L there is a lower bound of what a linear model can do, and no model can be credited with skill beyond linear on this dataset

synthetic:rossler: independent check: F + L at step 1 measured on the scored windows is 3.495 nats; read from the history's spectrum without forecasting it (the price of naivety) it is between 1.594 and 3.072 nats; the measured value is outside that range, so read the step-1 rungs with care

synthetic:seasonal_trend: at steps 1 the linear model's squared error is 287 times smaller than repeating the last value: the series is nearly deterministic (smooth or periodic). There the attainable linear gain has no finite bound (it is set by the noise floor and by how much memory the model gets), so read these rungs as 'almost perfectly forecastable' rather than as a precise amount, and compare models by ratios, not by percentages, which are all close to 100%.

trust: Every score, including the ladder's rungs, goes through one function (horizoneval.evaluate); there is no second way to compute a number.

That scoring reproduces published results: all 98 numbers of the official M4 table and all 400 GIFT-Eval leaderboard numbers of seasonal naive and naive (results/replication-m4, results/replication-gift-eval).

The ladder reproduces its paper's calibration: on series with a known optimum the linear rung recovers the true value (0.298 against 0.288 nats) and the exact optimal model is never credited with skill beyond linear (0 of 12 seeds; results/replication-ladder, horizoneval replicate ladder).
The decision statistics (probability of best, winner's curse, verified claims) are checked by simulation on cases with known answers (horizoneval.verify, tests/).
